title: A 'Black Hole Star' in the Early Universe
hook: JWST found something from the universe's first few hundred million years that looks like a giant star but shines a hundred billion times too brightly to be one.
key_points: The object dates from just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang and appears very red in JWST's infrared images.
Its spectrum resembles a star's, but its luminosity is around 100 billion times what a star can produce.
The proposed explanation: a black hole of roughly 100,000 solar masses wrapped in a dense cocoon of hydrogen.
The cocoon is about the size of the solar system, and it is the cocoon — not the black hole — that produces the star-like spectrum.
Such objects would offer a route to growing supermassive black holes fast enough to match the ones JWST sees early on.
content_html: James Webb has turned up an object from a few hundred million years after the Big Bang that does not fit either of the usual categories. Its light looks stellar — the sort of spectrum a giant star produces — yet it is roughly 100 billion times brighter than any star could be. Astronomers have nicknamed it a "black hole star."
extra_html:
The favoured explanation is that a black hole of around 100,000 solar masses sits inside a dense cocoon of hydrogen about the size of our solar system. The black hole supplies the energy; the surrounding envelope is what actually radiates, and it does so with the absorption features that make the object look like an enormous star. The disguise is the point — this is a black hole hiding behind stellar clothing.

If the interpretation holds, it matters beyond one odd source. JWST has repeatedly found black holes that look too massive for how early they appear, and a hidden massive black hole already gorging inside a gas envelope is one way to build up to supermassive scales fast enough. See ScienceDaily's report for the discovery details.

related.title: 31 Quasars That Are Too Old to Make Sense
related.hook: Astronomers found 31 quasars shining from when the universe was just 5% of its current age — powered by black holes that shouldn't have had time to grow so big yet.

related.title: Did Clusters of Primordial Black Holes Seed JWST's Puzzling 'Little Red Dots'?
related.hook: JWST found overweight black holes far too early in the universe for standard theories to explain. One proposal: they were seeded by swarms of black holes born moments after the Big Bang.

related.title: Black Holes
related.hook: A black hole is a place where gravity wins so completely that nothing — not even light — can escape once it crosses the edge called the event horizon.

related.title: Why Does Webb Keep Finding Things That Shouldn't Exist?
related.hook: JWST keeps spotting early black holes and galaxies that are too big, too bright, or too early to fit standard models — and cosmologists are racing to figure out which of many new theories is right.

flashcards.prompt: Why can't the 'black hole star' simply be an unusually large star?
flashcards.back_html: Its spectrum looks stellar, but it shines roughly 100 billion times more brightly than a star can. No star can sustain that output — something other than fusion has to be powering it.

flashcards.prompt: In the proposed model, what produces the object's star-like appearance?

choices.text: A dense hydrogen cocoon, about the size of the solar system, wrapped around a black hole
A cluster of millions of ordinary stars blurred together by distance
A supernova caught mid-explosion, briefly mimicking a stellar spectrum

flashcards.explanation_html: The black hole — around 100,000 solar masses — supplies the power, but the surrounding envelope of hydrogen is what radiates, giving the object a deceptively stellar spectrum.

flashcards.prompt: Why are objects like this interesting for the puzzle of early supermassive black holes?
flashcards.back_html: JWST keeps finding very massive black holes very early in cosmic history. A massive black hole already fed by a dense envelope offers a way to reach those masses in the short time available.
